opus-5.5.text:
So the classical picture in formal semantics, going back to Montague, says the meaning of a sentence is something like its truth conditions. You have a logical form, and you evaluate it against a model of the world, some set of entities and relations, to decide whether it's true. That's a beautiful and very powerful framework. It gives you compositionality almost for free, and it handles quantifiers, negation and scope well.

What always bothered me is that the "world" in that picture is a hand-built abstraction. Someone has already decided what the entities are, what the predicates are, and what "red" or "left of" picks out. All the hard grounding work is assumed rather than explained. When you want to build a system that actually perceives an image, or acts in an environment, or follows instructions, that assumption is where everything breaks.

What I wanted to do, starting around my PhD work on neural module networks and related projects, was keep what's right about formal semantics while learning the parts that touch the world. Keep compositional structure, the idea that meanings are built from smaller pieces that combine in predictable ways. But let the denotations of those pieces be learned functions over real perceptual input or real environment states. Instead of "red" being a symbol in a hand-specified model, it's a little learned module that looks at pixels and highlights the red things. Instead of a parser producing a logical form you evaluate symbolically, you produce a structured computation you can actually execute against data.

More broadly, I wanted to treat grounding as something learned from use, from paired language and observations or language and outcomes, rather than stipulated. Increasingly that's also pushed me the other way: asking whether large models trained mostly on text end up building something like those world models internally, and whether we can find and inspect that structure. So it's the same question from both directions. How do you get from symbols to a world you can reason about, without someone handing you the world in advance?

r001.rationale: The response says the world model, entities, predicates, and word meanings were hand-built, so grounding was assumed rather than explained.

r002.rationale: It describes learned denotations and a parser that produces executable computations, but does not clearly state that learning the language-to-representation mapping and the representations’ execution semantics happens jointly.

r003.rationale: It identifies neural module networks, says language is parsed into executable structured computation, and describes the meanings as learned functions over perceptual input rather than fixed symbolic denotations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I started grad school, the dominant way of thinking about this problem in the formal semantics tradition was that you take a sentence and you map it to some logical form, some expression in a formal language, and then that logical form is the thing that gets interpreted against the world. And there's a lot that's really appealing about that picture. You get compositionality for free, you get a very clean story about how the meanings of words combine into the meanings of sentences, and you get something you can actually execute, so you can hand it to a database or a planner and get an answer back.

But the thing that always bothered me was that the formal language itself was doing an enormous amount of work that nobody was really accounting for. Somebody had to sit down and decide what the predicates were, what the primitives were, what the ontology of the world looked like. And that decision was being made by a human, usually by the person building the system, before any learning happened. So the "grounding" part, the part where language actually touches the world, had been sort of hidden inside the representation. You'd learn a mapping from English to logic, but the mapping from logic to perception, or to action, was fixed by hand.

And that felt backwards to me, because it's exactly the hard part. If you look at a picture or you're moving around in an environment, the right set of concepts to carve the world up with isn't given to you. It depends on what you need to talk about and what you need to do. So what I wanted to do was keep the good parts of the formal semantics story, the compositionality, the idea that sentence structure tells you how to assemble meaning, but make the primitives learnable. Instead of a fixed inventory of logical predicates, you'd have modules, or little pieces of a neural network, whose behavior is learned from data, and the structure of the sentence tells you how to wire those pieces together.

So the sentence still gets parsed into something that looks a lot like a logical form. But rather than evaluating that form against a symbolic model of the world, you treat it as a blueprint for building a function, and that function operates directly on pixels or on the state of an environment. The syntax gives you the shape of the computation and the learning gives you the content. That's really the shift I was after: moving the grounding problem out of a hand-written ontology and into something you can actually learn end to end, without throwing away the structure that makes language so efficient in the first place.

r001.rationale: It says the mapping from logic to perception or action was fixed by hand and that the grounding work was hidden inside the representation.

r002.rationale: It says the language-to-logic mapping was learned, then separately proposes learning the modules that execute the representation. It does not clearly state that both are learned jointly.

r003.rationale: It describes sentence structure wiring together learned neural modules that operate on pixels or environment state, replacing a fixed inventory of predicates with learnable primitives.

astra-6.text:
The thing I wanted to change was how much of that connection had to be specified by hand. In a traditional formal semantics setup, you might map a sentence into a logical expression, and then interpret that expression against a database or a model of the world. That gives you a very precise account of how meanings compose. But somebody still has to decide what the predicates are and how they connect to things in the world.

I was interested in whether we could learn more of that connection from data. Could a system observe language alongside images or actions and learn what the pieces of the language refer to, while preserving the compositional structure that makes formal approaches useful? The goal was to bring together that structure and the ability to learn from messier observations.

r001.rationale: The response says predicates and their connections to the world must be decided by hand, but does not state that execution semantics were assumed to be known in advance.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning language references from data while preserving compositional structure, but does not clearly propose jointly learning execution semantics and the mapping into executable meaning representations.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention ModuleNets or describe language-conditioned structured computation with primitives unspecified in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I wanted to broaden what we meant by connecting language to the world. In a lot of formal semantics, you start with a neatly specified world—a database, say—and the task is to turn a sentence into a logical expression that you can evaluate against it. That gives you a very precise account of meaning, but it leaves open how those symbols connect to perception and action.

The question that interested me was whether we could keep that compositional structure while learning the pieces from data. Could the meaning of a word be a computation over an image, or something that helps an agent decide what to do? Then understanding a sentence means assembling those pieces into a computation that actually interacts with the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluating logical expressions against a specified world, but does not clearly say that the representations’ execution semantics were known in advance.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning word meanings from data, but does not clearly describe jointly learning execution semantics and the mapping from language into representations.

r003.rationale: It describes assembling learned meanings into computations, but does not identify ModuleNets or state that their primitive operations need not be specified in advance.
